In connection with the work done by the inspectors, there has been considerable adverse criticism of the system. Would the minister inform us how the system has worked ?

speechtext: I observe that on this page there are, I think, 24 items altogether and with respect to 13 of them the Civil Service Act is repealed pro tanto. Does the hon. gentleman think that is a desirable style of legislation-to have an Act which is repealed with regard to any particular item whenever it is found convenient to repeal it ? The estimates are sent up to the other House under a conditiou that they must either accept the whole appropriation Bill or reject the whole of it. I have brought the matter to the attention of the House on other occasions, and I cannot allow this to pass without putting in my protest against this practical repeal of the Civil Service Act. The Act should be amended if it cannot be observed. It does not seem to me to be a good system, and I do not think my hon. friend will say it is a good system to pursue with reference to this Act.

There is a great deal in what my hon. friend says. But at the same time he will see that often great inequalities have crept Hon. Mr. BERNIER.
into the payments of many of these officers. In the case of Mr. Nutting, for a considerable number of years he received no increase at all, and this is virtually giving him the statutory increases which in the ordinary course he would have been receiving. In the other case it is only a statutory increase of $50. But this gentleman had been, as I understand, at the head of the second service class for a considerable time, and when he was put into my department and given charge of a rather important branch, it was thought the least we could do would be to give him $50 as well- as the rank of first-class clerk. While I candidly admit that both legally and otherwise the hon. gentleman is right and we ought not to have so many of these cases, still these are very small sins, as he will observe.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
These are the pin-pricks which make our life intolerable on this side of the House. I want to say to my hon. friend that I am not finding any fault with these gentlemen, or criticising the increases to them in any way, for I have no doubt they are capable gentlemen and deserving of the increases granted. My remarks are applicable to the system. It seems to me a bad system, and that we would do better to amend the Act so as to confer some greater discretion, if necessary, on the different departments, than to repeal it from time to time in a way which prevents the Upper House from dealing with it. I am not sure that the Senate would not be perfectly justified in throwing out the whole appropriation Bill on this account. They are not supposed to amend that Bill at all, but must either reject or accept it in its entirety. The result is that an Act which they have passed is being repealed by this House in such a way that they have not one word as to the wisdom or unwisdom of the proposed repeal. That is net a satisfactory way of conducting legislation, and I am glad that, so far as the principle is concerned, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce agrees in the view I have stated.

speechtext:
I was about to ask whether there had been anything done to define our rights in the fisheries, under the decision of the Privy Council. A few years ago the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council decided that the fisheries belonged to the provinces with the exception j of some ocean fisheries, and we naturally 1 expected that there would be a reduction

in the cost of looking after them. Last year, however, there was an increase in the item of salaries and disbursements of fishery inspectors, overseers, and guardians amounting to $15,000, instead of a decrease, and I notice that this year the item is $85,000, the same as last. Has the government reached any agreement with the provinces as to the rights we have or the duties we are required to perform ? And would it not be possible to reduce the expenditure on this item in view of the fact that the fisheries have been declared to be the property of the provinces ? There ought to be some understanding between the Dominion and the several provinces on this matter.

There really has been no progress made since last session with regard to this matter. The decision of the Privy Council is difficult to understand. So far as I have been able to inform myself, after looking into the communications between the different provinces and the department, the parties seem to be further away from an agreement as to the meaning of this matter than when they started. It appears to me, not being a lawyer, that this matter will have to be settled by one or other of two courses. So far as the present condition of affairs, it is certainly very unsatisfactory. Either the points in dispute must be referred to some tribunal for settlement, aud both the Dominion and the provinces must abide by that decision, or there must be a conference and an agreement reached satisfactory to both parties. Before coming directly to the estimates, I may say that we all recognize the great importance of the fisheries of the Dominion and the necessity of having proper regulations to govern them. This one point is not in dispute-that the power to regulate the fisheries remains within the jurisdiction of the Dominion. That being the case, I think all will agree that, until some arrangement is made, it is the duty of the Dominion to see that the regulations are enforced and the fisheries protected. With regard to the item to which my hon. friend referred, that of $85,000, I find that at the time the judgment was given, the minister reduced the item, for some reason or other, by $25,000 or $30,000. It so remained, I think, for two years. But the expenditure remained the Lame as it had been an,d the result 'was a deficit* which, I believe, was made up bv a supplementary vote last session. After careful investigation it is found that nothing less than $85,000 would do for this item. Previously, I think, it was $90,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I think it is very desirable indeed that any difficulties with regard to the relative position of the Dominion and the provinces, if there are any such, should be settled at ouce. I have not recently examined the judgment of the Privy Council and am not sure now how

far it goes. But I think that the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries, during last session of parliament, told us that negotiations were to be had, or a further case submitted to the courts for the purpose of determining certain further questions. I may point out to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. James Sutherland) that the matter is of some immediate importance, because, as I understand, the provinces are about making a claim upon the government of Canada in respect of the fisheries award. I believe that the Attorney General of the province of New Brunswick has recently announced to the people of that province in an election manifesto that he proposed to make, or has made, a formal claim on this government for a portion of that award. If, while we are subject to a claim of that kind, we continue to pay for services, which, perhaps, legitimately belong to the different provinces, we are, certainly, not pursuing a very wise course. If these difficulties and uncertainties exist I would suggest to the hon. minister that he should lose no time in putting himself in communication with the Department of Justice aud having a matter so serious dealt with at once.

In the decision of the Privy Council on this question and others that were submitted by the Dominion and the provinces, there are specific findings that it is well to understand. It was contended on the part of the Dominion that the Dominion had the proprietary right in certain of the fisheries. That was settled adversely to the Dominion, it being held that proprietary right of the fisheries were vested in the provinces or in the individuals who possessed the same at the time of the British North America Act. But it was also held that the Dominion has absolute control, so far as the regulating is concerned, and that in regulating, they can interfere to any extent with the proprietary rights, except to the extent of granting an absolute right of fishery to other parties. It is also decided that the Dominion, under subsections 3 and 12, has the right to raise a revenue by taxation on the fisheries by way of license, and that the provinces have a similar right. The whole question is reduced by that judgment, as I understand it, to this-that the Dominion government has the sole right to regulate the fisheries and the provinces cannot interfere with that in the slightest degree. Thus, the Department of Marine and Fisheries is left in the same position as before in this matter and must make the same expenditure as before, in order to enforce the law, because this parliament is the only parliament that has power to make regulations about the fisheries. Back of this, there is a question that may arise in the future, and that is whether the Dominion has or has not, in days past, undertaken to give an exclusive right of fishery when they

granted licenses for the use of traps and other engines for the capture of flsh. If they did so, the question arises whether the parties who paid these license fees supposing that they were receiving exclusive rights of fishery would have a claim upon the Dominion for the refund of that money. But this does not question in any way the obligation upon the department to make and enforce fishery* regulations, for. in that respect, the provinces are absolutely powerless.

I take it that a great part of what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wade) has told us was generally known. What I wished to know was whether any effort was being made to have a conference with the provinces with a view to a determination of the powers of either side.

There have been a great many negotiations in this direction. I may explain that, by agreement, we still receive all the revenues, except from the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, pending final arrangements. Negotiations have gone so far that we have in the department now a memorandum from the province of Quebec of a case that they would like us to join in submitting to the courts. The province of Quebec also has recently sent a very formidable statement of claim with regard to the province's rights in the matter. I agree with the leader of the opposition that, as soon as possible, some conclusion must be come to with regard to these difficulties. It will probably be slow work at the best, but it is my intention, as far as I can, with the assistance of the Department of Justice, to put the matter in shape and have it settled.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Who issues the licenses, the Dominion or the provinces ?
The province, in the case of Ontario and Quebec ; but, in the other provinces, the Dominion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I understood the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) to say that it was clearly decided by the Privy Council that both the province and the Dominion have the right to raise revenue from the fisheries. In what way does the Dominion propose to raise a revenue to recoup us for looking after the fisheries and control-ing them ?

That is one of the matters that parliament has to decide after these other matters are settled. We have not taken action to make up the loss of revenue. If the hon. gentleman had understood me he would have understood that we have receipts as formerly, except from Ontario and Quebec. Last year these receipts were about .$45,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Although under the decision, territorial rights or powers are held by the provinces it does not in any way relieve the Dominion from the obligation it is under to protect the fisheries. The Dominion has all the powers to regulate and even to restrain the fishery rights and carrying with it those powers certainly it carries with it the onus of protection. Now, in the province of New Brunswick they have enacted legislation giving power to the government to enter into negotiations and to lease the territorial rights to the Dominion. It would seem to me to be in the best interests of the provinces generally and indeed of the Dominion that the Dominion should control and should have all the fishery rights, even to the territorial rights. From the standpoint of the Dominion and from the standpoint of our trade and navigation all interests combine and unite in pointing to the Dominion as the proper authority. Under these circumstances it would seem to me that it would be wise on the part of the Department of Marine and Fisheries to conclude negotiations at as early a date as convenient and where possible with the several provinces with a view of acquiring the rights of the provinces.

I want to say in connection with this matter that I understand that we have the right to regulate and protect the fisheries ; that is to say the size of the mesh of the net, to regulate the close season and to prescribe the kind of fish traps to be used. But, the question is : If we get no revenue from it, is it worth our while to protect the fisheries all over the country ? If we have the right over and above the provinces to raise a revenue upon the sale of fishing licenses or from some other source had we not better avail ourselves of it, because otherwise the Dominion will be paying out money for doing the work of the provinces ? As this decision has been given some time ago, it would seem to be desirable for the government to endeavour at the earliest possible moment to reach some conclusion with the provinces in regard to the rights we have, the duties we must perform and where the revenue will come from to pay the expenses incurred in protecting the fisheries.

I would like to draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that the Dominion has been collecting a revenue from these fisheries for years by selling licenses to parties to fish with seines and fish traps. All along the coast of Nova Scotia these licenses have been sold by the Dominion authorities and the revenue derived from them has come to the Dominion.
Mr. SPROL'LE. The question is whether the Dominion shall be permitted to retain that revenue.

The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) must understand the dif-

Acuity in the distribution of powers. It is not an easy matter with a question over which the local legislature may have a partial authority and in which the Dominion may have rights to decide it as quickly as the hon. gentleman thinks. But, what I rose to say was that I dissent entirely from the proposition he makes : It is no difference if the Dominion has only such power to look after our fisheries, it must not do it unless it gets a revenue out of it. That is a proposition, I think, which must not be entertained for a moment. If the Dominion alone can do certain things it makes no difference whether we get a revenue or not. The Dominion must do it in the interests of the fisheries and the people of Canada. You cannot decide a question by saying that it simply costs so much and we must get so much for performing this duty or we will not do anything at all.

I did not pretend to advocate any such doctrine. What I suggested was that if the provinces get all the revenue and all the advantages from the fisheries, would it not be desirable to have a conference with the provinces and to decide who shall assume the full responsibility of protecting the fisheries.

The government can only do what they have power to do. The argument, if I understand it, meant, that while the power might be inherent in one parliament to do a certain thing, unless it paid, parliament should not do it.
The hon. gentleman must not forget that the decision explicitly said that we had joint powers with the provinces.
Very able lawyers differ about what it means.
They always do.

There is this anomaly, that while the territorial right is in the provinces, the Dominion may adopt regulations making entirely valueless these territorial rights; in other words, the Dominion, under its powers, can, by regulation, absolutely prohibit and restrain the use of a river in respect to its fisheries, and yet the territorial right is in the provinces.
A stronger reason for coming- to an amicable understanding.

I quite agree with what the hon. gentleman says with respect to the desirability of coming to an arrangement, but pending such the Dominion must expend the money in order to protect the fisheries and carry out the regulations, it alone having the power. The provinces have no power in that direction at all.

Would the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) kindly tell us at what time that legislation was Mr. FRASER.
passed in New Brunswick to which he referred ?

I am really pleased to hear the hon. gentleman saying this. That is not the tune we got in Charlotte when he was running his last election. The tune there which was sung to the poor fishermen was this : These are the fellows that will have you by the throat if you do not vote for the local government. To-day he has changed his tune, and it is a very different story to that which we heard in the election.

In connection with this question, I desire to offer an observation or two. We had a very interesting decision by the Supreme Court of Prince Edward Island in regard to this question a few days ago. The farmers of Prince Edward Island have for the last twenty or thirty years been digging mussel mud in the beds of the rivers for the purpose of fertilizing their farms. A regulation was passed by the department that no farmer should use his mud machine within 200 yards of a live oyster bed. They submitted to that, but now we find the department has placed an arbitrary line across certain rivers restricting the farmers from using this mussel mud for the purpose of fertilizing their farms. While the oyster fishery in Prince Edward Island is a very important fishery, the farming industry is also equally important, and if you restrict the farmer from taking his mussel mud within 200 yards of the live oyster bed, you will give full protection to the oyster fishery. The decision in the Supreme Court was this : Up the North river, I remember very well, au oyster fishery, or a bed for the protection of the oyster, was set aside by the government of Canada some years ago. A farmer in the prosecution of his industry came along and placed his mud digger within the limits as laid down by the government of Canada. Now, we wish to protect this oyster fishery, but you will see that you have an oyster bed of so many hundred yards square. You have a live oyster bed that must be protected by the government, but can you prevent the farmer from coming along and prosecuting his industry in the vicinity of that oyster bed ? It is true the Supreme Court of Prince Edward Island decided that the government of Canada had the right to pass these rules and regulations, but if they were to be enforced, every farmer would be debarred from getting this valuable fertilizer in the vicinity of these oyster beds. I asked the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries a question a few days ago in connection with the lines drawn across the rivers in Prince Edward Island. Is it the intention on the Trout river and the Biddeford river in Prince county that no farmer shall be allowed to take mussel mud except within the lines he has defined ?

In reply to the hon. gentleman, 1 would say that when he brought the matter to my attention the other day and when another application was made to the department, I looked into it and came to the conclusion that a good deal of discretion might be used in enforcing these regulations. I gave instructions to the principal officer of the department in charge on the island that he was not to enforce the regulations strictly unless it was really necessary to protect the oyster beds. I think we will all agree that it is necessary to protect the oyster beds, but otherwise I think a great deal of discretion can be left to the officers as to whether this practice will really destroy valuable beds or not. I have issued instructions to that effect.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: There is very little connection between the subject now under discussion in this committee and the elections which were held in New Brunswick in 1899.
Not just now, but there was then.

I fear that the hon. gentleman's memory fails him in respect to the attitude of the local government of that day. I can only say that the opinions which I have expressed here to-day were the opinions expressed by me, not merely in other counties in New Brunswick, but in the county of Charlotte. I know that my hon. friend (Mr. Ganong) feels a little sore with respect to that election, because he failed to carry out the pledge which he gave to the celebrated Moncton convention to send four Conservatives to the New Brunswick Legislature. That pi'obably is a sore spot with him.

I have to say that while the hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) does not mean to misrepresent me, his statement is absolutely untrue. I do not place the responsibility at the doors of my hon. friend, because I do not believe he would make the statement if he knew it to be untrue. Whether the hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) made the statement or not, these men who followed him and did his work certainly said so, for I was at their meeting when they did say it.
I spoke there at three different places.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) was like the ex-Minister of Marine ; instead of talking to fishermen he went to talk to the farmers. That was usually the way down there.
I talked with pretty good effect in the county of Charlotte.

Do I understand that Ontario and Quebec issue licenses and refuse to pay the revenue over to the Dominion
Treasury while the other provinces do pay us the revenue.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) is practically correct if not technically so. So far as the other provinces are concerned we go on collecting the revenue by arrangement just as in the past. This vote amounts to some $300,000, and even if all the provinces collected the revenue, the House might come to the conclusion that it was desirable to vote money for the protection of the fisheries, the management of fish breeding establishments and so on. The hon. gentleman is quite correct in saying that Ontario and Quebec now collect the license fees, which formerly brought in a revenue of some $40,000 or $45,000 per annum to the Dominion, and we do not now receive any revenue from that source in these two provinces.
speakername: The MINISTER OF SIARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: This appropriation is for the purpose of protecting the fisheries, and I wish to draw the attention of the Minister to what is now being done on Lake Erie. Before the province of Ontario took hold of the fishing rights the Dominion government limited the number of licenses ; but 1 am informed that the Ontario government proposes now to increase the number of licenses by some sixty or seventy along the Lake Erie front. If that is done it will be only a matter of a year or two when the valuable fishing grounds there are depleted. If. the Dominion government had any control over the matter I could understand that we should vote money for the protection of the fisheries whose duty it would or ought to be to protect the fisheries and that can be done largely by limiting the number of licenses.

I want to say that this question of the protection of the oyster fishery, and allowing the farmers of Prince Edward Island to take mussel mud in the rivers is a very important question with us. The minister said that in connection with these two lines drawn across the Trout river and the Biddeford river, that the enforcement of that arrangement will be left entirely to the discretion of the local officers. You have quite a sufficient quantity of mussel mud for the use of farmers irrespective and clear altogether of the oyster beds. The first duty of this government is to protect the oyster fisheries and at the same time they can allow the farmer to prosecute his industry by getting this valuable fertilizer from the beds of our rivers. If you allow this matter to rest altogether in the hands of the local officers you may have partisanship. You may have one man digging mussel mud and taking it to his farm, while another man of a different political stripe will be prohibited from doing so. The government should not allow this matter to remain altogether in the hands of the local officers.

The authority of the inspector in Prince Edward Island to exercise his discretion in this matter is subject to the approval of the department. I do not think there can be any partisanship because the officer once he decides that they can take mussel mud out of a certain place, cannot interfere with any one from taking it there.
speakername: Tlie MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: This vote includes the salary of a certain official residing in the county of Hastings, who had the honour of representing East Hastings for one parliament, who at the last general elections was defeated by the electors, and who shortly after that was appointed to the position of Inspector of Fisheries. I refer to Mr. Hurley, the ex-member for East Hastings. I understand that the principle is laid down by the government, that officials of the government should not take an active part in elections, and certain officers have been dismissed because it was alleged they did take an active part in politics. I wish to state that this official to whom I have referred, during the late by-election in the adjoining riding of West Hastings, was found to be active during the whole of that election. I am happy to say that his efforts to defeat the Conservative candidate were not successful. I am, however, unhappy to say that a petition has been lodged protesting the result of that election, and this officer whom I have mentioned, was, I am informed, upon authority on which I can safely rely, the very gentleman who solicited the petitioner to sign the petition against the return of the present member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter). I wish now to ask from the hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Sutherland). I know much of this vote is intended to pay the inspector of fisheries for his duties as inspector, and what proportion of it is intended to remunerate him for the part he took in the late election.

That is a very good principle, if carried out impartially, but not if it be used merely for the purpose of dismissing office holders whose political convictions are opposed to those of the party in power. That doctrine laid down by the leader of the government has been frequently applied in my own constituency. speechtext: Before the item passes, I would like to ascertain the views of the Minister of Justice with regard to the necessity of having questions as to the respective rights of the Dominion and the provinces in the fisheries again submitted to the courts. I understood the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries to tell us last year that it was, in his opinion, necessary, or, at least, desirable, that some other question should be submitted. I think, also, he expressed his intention of having that course adopted at an early day. From the views that have been put forward by my hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Wade) and my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson), apparently the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries was not correct in the views he then expressed. I would like to know the views of the Minister of Justice with regard to that, and whether he considers it necessary to adopt such a course.

The judgment of the Privy Council, is in my opinion, extremely confused and indistinct. In fact, were I not speaking of a decision of the highest court of the empire, I would be tempted to say that it is self-contradictory in its terms. However, I think we can safely say that there are two points which are firmly and clearly established. One is that the provinces have all the territorial powers as regards fisheries, and the other- but I had better read from the text so as to have it absolutely correct:-
That the enactment of fishery regulations and restrictions is within the exclusive competence of the Dominion legislature and is not within the powers of the provincial legislatures.
Therefore, we have this condition of things, it seems to me, that the territorial rights as regards the fisheries are vested in I the provinces and that the regulating of

the fisheries is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Dominion parliament. Now, in my view, speaking without very much preparation on the subject, I would be inclined to consider that the federal government can, irrespective of locality, declare that no one shall fish generally without paying a fishing fee or tax to the department; that they can also determine the close season, regulate the size of boats, license the boats-they can do all those things that have reference to the general regulation of the fisheries. Coming to the special question which the leader of the opposition has put, I would be disposed to say that the Dominion and the provinces might get together and, through their representatives, come to an agreement as to how this judgment is to be construed. If they are not prepared to do that, then, because of the vague and indistinct terms in which the judgment is couched it will be necessary to submit further questions to the court for the purpose of construing the judgment of the Privy Council.
Does my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) understand that the duty of protection would follow the territorial rights or the power of regulation ?

I think that would follow the power of regulation. In fact, I think there are very much larger powers vested in the Dominion than is at the present time generally admitted.. I think the provinces are under an entirely erroneous impression with regard to this judgment. They are told virtually, if I may interpret the judgment: You are the proprietors of this property, but you have no control over it. I think the sooner we define and settle these questions the better for all concerned. The present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. James Sutherland) has begun discussing the matter with the department ; and, if I -may say so, I am ready to take the matter up and have it disposed of almost immediately. It may be anomalous to ask a court to construe its own judgment, but if we are forced to that *conclusion, the fault is not entirely ours.

There is one *other matter I would like to say a word about, and to this I would ask the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. It is a matter I brought to the attention of the late minister. In a great many cases we find very small salaries paid to fishery inspectors accompanied by very large travelling expenses. At page P-109, of the Auditor General's Report, we find a salary of $218.75 accompanied with a charge of $746 for travelling expenses ; another salary of $187.50 with travelling expenses of $507.05. On the following page we find ' salary, $175 ; travel, $562.73.' And on the same page a salary of $187.50 is accom-184
panied by travelling expenses of $603.01. The explanation made by the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries last year was that the travelling expenses were really a part of the salary ; that the inspector went out with his own horse and buggy, and sent in vouchers as if he had spent so much money in travelling, though, in fact, he had spent no money, but had used his own conveyance.
I think it would be better to put these things on a proper basis. If this is part of the salary let it be paid as part of the salary and not entered as fictitious travelling expenses.

It is quite true, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) says that comparatively small salaries are accompanied by comparatively large charges for travelling expenses. I am assured by the officers of the department that these matters are very closely scrutinized, and that in no case that may be investigated will it be found that these are paid as part of a salary. The districts, in some cases, are very large, and the inspectors have to travel by hiring horses and rigs. They are allowed a fixed rate of ten cents per mile of travel, twenty-five cents for each meal, twenty-five cents for horse-feed, and twenty-five cents for a bed. These accounts are sent in and sworn to by the parties, and are carefully investigated by the department. Whether any other system can be adopted that will be better while securing equal efficiency, I could not say. I will look into the matter.

speechtext:
Before this item is carried, I would like to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that the results which have attended so far the initiation of the cold storage system in Nova Scotia have been more gratifying than we could have anticipated. I wish to point out to the government that if we are going to deal with this great question of bait supply for what is perhaps the greatest industry We have in the maritime provinces, an industry which would represent $15,000,000 annually, we cannot stop at the point we have now reached. The bait freezers at present in operation are principally to serve the wants of the shore fisheries while no provision has been made for the bank fisheries. Of course, the stores in these small freezers can be drawn upon by the bank fishermen, but when we take into consideration the enormous loss entailed every year by the bank fishermen it will be seen that something more will have to be done. I would' throw out by way of suggestion that in my humble opinion it would be a paying thing for the country and for thel government to establish one freezer at a cost of about $35,000 or $40,000 at some important point along the Atlantic coast where bait could be most easily procured, in order that five or six hundred vessels, some large and some small, would be enabled to obtain a sufficient supply of bait. I think there is no doubt that our losses would average at least anywhere from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 yearly from the want of this accommodation. I wish to point out also to the government that the adjoining colony of Newfoundland is now arranging for the installation of a bait plant there. If we are to compete with the Newfoundland fisheries, we must be thoroughly supplied with bait as are the Newfoundland fishermen. I would point out that our competitors from Gloucester, New York, and Boston have also constant supplies of frozen

bait on band. It is a matter of prime importance that perhaps the largest industry, except agriculture, in the maritime provinces, should be accommodated with all necessary adjuncts for its successful operation. There is another matter to which I wish to call the attention of the House. I wish to point out that the freight receipts from the growing fresh fish trade from the maritime provinces to the west are increasing and increasing rapidly. I will give you one instance. Four years ago one firm, probably the largest of the fish firms, paid $10,000 in railway freights from the Straits of Oanso ; next year it paid $12,000 ; next year $14,000, and last year it paid, I think, $20,000. Let me say also that the facilities at the railway terminals in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are not what they should be. Before we can meet the requirements of the fresh fish trade we must have a few small refrigerators costing anywhere from $1,500 to $2,500 at the principal railway terminals in the maritime provinces.
Do you refer to mechanical cold storage ?

No. As far as I can understand the mechanical cold storage is more economical when you freeze over 800 tons, but under that, the idea seems to prevail that ice and salt is more economical.
I repeat what I said last year, that on the Intercolonial Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway the cold storage cars provided are not what they should be. Numbers of these cars are defective in construction. At some other time I shall draw attention to this matter, but I may state now in passing, that a great number of the cold storage cars on Canadian railways are not in a sanitary condition. It is also true that many of the refrigerators in Canada are not in a saui-tary condition and very frequently meat and fish transported arrive in a semi-putrid condition. I am nevertheless of the opinion that the results from our system of cold storage have been very gratifying up to the present time, and I beg to urge upon the government that they should grapple with this larger question which is certainly one of very great concern to a large proportion of the population of the maritime provinces -a population which seems inclined to remain by the fishing industry, and which I regret to say is very much inclined indeed to move to the United States.

I corroborate the statement made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kendall). Some few years ago, that hon. gentleman (Mr. Kendall) came to Prince Edward Island for the purpose of establishing these bait freezers and the undertaking has proved a complete success. If there was nothing else done by the government during their period of office to assist the fishermen of the maritime provinces, the establishment
of these bait freezers has been a great boon to them. On the coasts of our maritime provinces, we have fishermen who must go out to sea in their small boats, and if they have not proper bait they cannot succeed in their calling. Gentlemen from the other provinces may not think much of the bait freezing experiment, but it has undoubtedly proved a great boon to the fishermen of the provinces by the sea. I would like to call the attention of the government to the fact, that after a shore fisherman catches the fish he must have some appliances whereby he can cure his fish properly for the West Indian and other markets. I believe that the government should do something in the way of providing patent driers to assist the fishermen in carrying out their industry. If you have these driers you will have the fish cured in proper condition, so that it can fairly compete with other fish in the markets of the world. That is especially true of the province of Prince Edward Island where, because of the sandy and loamy soil, and damp weather causing evaporation, the fish becomes dark when sun dried, and do not take the position on the markets which they should take. I trust that in addition to the bait freezers, the government will see its way clear to assist the fishermen in getting these patent driers.

I am pleased to hear the remarks of my hon. friend from Gape Breton (Mr. Kendall) and also to hear an endorsement of the benefits which these bait freezers have conferred. I think the proposition of my hon. friend is a practical one, and while I promised probably to do a good deal, I certainly feel that the subject he has brought before the House, and the suggestion he has made is a very important one, and it will have early consideration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Perhaps I may be in a better position to speak on this vote than some of the other members of the House, because I have invested some $15,000 in mechanical cold storage for precisely the purpose that is referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Kendall). There is no question but that this scheme can be carried out, and I think the amount the hon. gentleman suggests probably would be sufficient. I believe a cold storage plant that would cost $35,000 would probably freeze and care for, from two millions to three millions pounds of fish. You may wonder why I did not continue in the business, but I may say that the fish were running erratically for a year or two, and other matters demanded my attention. I may say, however, that the establishment built at White Head, Grand Manan, is still there and 1 have an engineer to look after it every year so that it will probably be running again. One year I successfully froze 750,000 pounds of fish. It was the year of the Spanish-American war and this fish was sold to American

fisherman. They sent boats to Grand Manan and bought the fish from the freezers, and carried them away in American bottoms. It occurred just about the time of the declaration of war, and the Gloucester fishermen were advised to throw their fish overboard and come home, which they did, fearing that some Spanish cruiser might tramp along the coast. I very much favour the proposition made by my hon. friend (Mr. Kendall) as it is one of the most important things which the government can possibly take up. There is a great deal of expense in connection with it. While there is a great difference between the initial cost of the fish and the price for which we can sell them, yet you have constantly to maintain your power and appliances, and with other attendant expenses the scheme gets too costly almost for a private corporation to take hold of. Up to the present time there is certainly some element of experiment in It.

I wish to recognize on behalf of the maritime provinces, the benefits we have derived during the initiation of these plants, from the services of Mr. J. F. Fraser, one of the engineers of the department. Mr. Fraser has given a degree of satisfaction that has made him the friend of every fisherman on these shores where he has visited. I also wish to observe that while we have had success in connection with a number of these freezers, we have not had success with regard to all. We have found it very difficult indeed to get the fishermen to co-operate. We started out with an ideal plan of putting the refrigerators in the hands of the fishermen themselves, but I am afraid that in some cases at least we will have to recede from that position and endeavour to enlist the sympathies of some business men.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kendall) what railways he is referring to when he speaks of the refrigerator cars being in an unsanitary condition. Does he include the refrU gerator cars on the Intercolonial Railway, or are there any such ?

There are some refrigerator cars on the Intercolonial Railway, and while I do not say that they are in an unsanitary condition, yet the construction of some of them is defective. I have seen cars arriving in Sydney and Glace Bay loaded with meat from large Ontario concerns and when the meat arrived, it certainly was not fit for food.

As far as many railways are concerned, we have no particular control over them, but in the case of the Intercolonial Railway we have something to say. If the hon. gentleman has anything to complain of with regard to the construction of the cars or the aecommo-
dation on the Intercolonial Railway, we should know it, so that we may bring that matter to the attention of the railway department.

It has been brought to the attention of that department.
Ottawa-Astronomical Observatory, $15,000.

Before this passes, I would like to remind the Minister of Public Works that last year he promised the Committee on Public Accounts that Mr. Charleson and Mr. Rochester and any other necessary witness would be present before that committee this year with all necessary vouchers. I would like to know whether or not he will be in a position to redeem that promise.

Mr. Charleson and Mr. Rochester are both in town and available as soon as the committee on Public Accounts meets. Mr. Boyer, one of the officers sent to the Yukon, will also be here a short time, and Mr. Tache.
How much has been expended and what will be the total expenditure on this item ?

We have not made much progress. The plans have been prepared and a site chosen on the experimental farm. But the plans prepared were too expensive, and new ones are being made for a building, the cost of which is not to exceed $40,000.
Ottawa-Branch of Royal Mint, $50,000.

The chief architect visited England, France and Belgium in order to obtain data for the preparation of plans. He has come back and prepared plans which have been sent to England and have not yet been returned. We are ready to begin the work now and are awaiting the return of the plans. The site chosen is on Nepean Point. The cost will be about $300,000.
I suppose the plans have to be approved by the Imperial authority ?
Yes, it is a branch of the Royal Mint.
Has the Minister decided whether this building is to be constructed on the day labour principle.

In every work yve have undertaken, we have always submitted our rates to the Labour Department, although perhaps at times that has caused us a lot of work and trouble. Still we have acted in good faith with the House.
Parliament buildings-addition to building over engine-house and improvements in main vestibule, including two electric elevators, $15,-
000.

I move that the words 'including two electric elevators' be struck out as these elevators are paid out of another appropriation. The SI 5,000 I am asking for is destined to provide further accommodation in the attic. I think the work carried on has been successful. We intend taking as many rooms as possible in the attic for members of parliament and replacing the old flooring by mosaic pavement.
Does this include the new building put up here ?

No, this is new work altogether not yet undertaken. If my hon. friend will go up stairs he will find that we will be able to give more accommodation by building rooms in the attic and continuing the work' wre have begun.
I suppose this is intended to induce us to live on another year on promises.
I am afraid my hon. friend lives too much In the past.

Last year we were promised a considerable number of rooms for the use of members, but this year we find very few more than last, although considerable extensions have been made. The [DOT]opposition have hardly been given their just rights and would like the Minister to do something more.

What I have done for the Opposition this year is not as much as I would like to have done, but I propose to do more later *on. I have consulted Mr. Speaker, and we have given a large room to the leader of the [DOT]opposition for the province of Quebec (Mr. Monk) and another room to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden). That makes two additional rooms for the opposition, and when we have built more rooms in the attic I think we will be able to gratify the wishes of our friends opposite. Our friends on this side complain just as bitterly and perhaps more so than my hon. friends opposite. We cannot give more than we have. We have built a very fine committee room. The debates reporters have been given nice quarters and their old room has been given to the Minister of Finance, who requires a large room as he receives large deputations.

As regards the distribution of the rooms, I think there might have been a better distribution without doing great injustice to any person. While on my feet, let me say that last year I understood that one of the objects of building this extension was to give a much larger committee room to the Railway Committee and allow the Railway Committee room to be
used by some other committee. I asked that the Agricultural Committee should be allowed to use the old Railway Committee room because it is the next largest committee to that of railways and because the room in which it has been the custom to meet is altogether too small. In fact it is impossible for its members to get seats when there is an average attendance. I suggested, at the last meeting of that committee, that we should use the old Railway Committee room, but was told that we could not be allowed the use of it for the present. There was no particular reason why we should not use it, and I would like to ask the hon. Minister whether it was not the intention, when providing this increased accommodation, to furnish larger rooms for the use of some of the larger committees.

Mr. Speaker has the right of distributing the rooms and I do not object to his doing so at all. I am prepared to give up all my privileges in that connection because they really give more trouble than pleasure. I am in the hands of the House. If the House prefers to deal with Mr. Speaker, I shall be delighted to give up all my rights immediately. If I am to distribute the rooms, I am prepared to be responsible, or I am quite ready to act jointly with Mr. Speaker. After the observations made, I do not see why the old committee room should not be used by jhe Committee on Agriculture, which is a very important committee. We have a large committee room up stairs, large enough to accommodate a considerable assembly of people. So, I do not see why the old committee room should not be used in the way pointed out.

It would hardly be convenient to have this room assigned exclusively to the Committee on Agriculture. There are other important committees, and they do not all meet on the same day. I should think that several committees could use this room, with a little adjustment. I would like it understood that such committees as that on Banking and Commerce, Public Accounts, and others, have equal rights.

I had no intention of suggesting that the Committee on Agriculture should have sole use of the room. The Committee on Public Accounts and possibly others might also use it, as they do not meet on the same days as the Committee on Agriculture. This room might accommodate two or three committees. As soon as the Minister of Public Works and Mr. Speaker come to a decision as to who has authority, we shall be able to discuss matters. It is easier to deal with one of these gentlemen than both. Both are very able, and I do not know with which of them I would prefer to deal. Heretofore we have always considered that Mr. Speaker has authority in these subjects.	,

56*
I have no objection.
When we find who has the authority, we will deal with him.

Did I understand the Minister of Public Works to say that when he got the plans for the Royal Mint he was going to construct that building by day labour ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WO'
No, it will be by tender-most decidedly.
How many additional rooms does the hon. minister hope to be able to provide in the attic of this building by the expenditure of this vote ?
The chief architect thought he would be able to provide four large rooms.
Will there be any further accommodation for hon. gentlemen on this side ?
I think we may speak of that when the rooms are ready. I will do the fair thing next year, as I have done this year.

There is another matter to which I wish to direct attention, and I am sure that I have only to mention it to have hon. gentlemen opposite agree with me. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition has a room about twenty feet long by ten feet wide. An hon. gentleman beside me suggests that it is six feet wide, and probably it is nearer six than ten. In the discharge of his important duties, the leader of the opposition, as hon. gentlemen opposite know, must receive a great many persons who desire to call upon him. He requires also the services of a stenographer. And, when I point out to the minister that when a gentleman calls upon the leader of the opposition on business, he must send his stenographer out to stand about in the lobby until the Interview is over, I think I say ail that is necessary to convince him that better accommodation is required for the leader of the opposition. The suggestion has been made-I do not know enough about the internal arrangement of the House to form an opinion as to whether it is practicable or not-that if the room between No. 6 and that occupied by the hon. leader of the opposition were vacated by the present occupant and added to the room which the leader of the opposition occupies, it might be used by his stenographer and also by some other members who have large correspondence and require some better accommodation to enable them to handle it. At any rate, I feel I can appeal to the hon. Minister of Public Works on behalf of the leader of the opposition to ask that better accommodation be provided.

I know very well that the hon. leader of the Mr. SPROULE.
opposition is not accommodated as he ought to be. It is true that all leaders of the opposition for the last twenty years have occupied the same room, but that does not make the case any better.
It is time for a change.

In some respects-yes. So far as the point referred to is concerned, I fully agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) that it is time for a change. The room allotted to the hon. leader of the opposition is so small that no ordinary business man would locate even a subordinate employee in it. His secretary must be in the same room and right at his side. When the new rooms are built upstairs, if my authority in the matter is admitted, I think I may find it possible, not by a general change, but by a pretty general change, to accommodate my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) as he has a right to be, and as the country has a right to expect that he will be accommodated.
Do I understand that that part of the vote relating to two electric elevators is struck out ?

Yes, the elevatots are built and are being paid for out of another appropriation.
Item, as amended, agreed to.
Public Works-chargeable to capital-public buildings-Ottawa-Victoria Memorial Museum, $50,000.
We would like some information about this.

I am sorry to say we have not done much yet. The chief architect has been away in connection with the Royal Mint, and we had so much on hand in the way of public buildings that we have not been able to proceed very fast. Moreover, there are difficulties in the way. The first difficulty is as to site. It was suggested last year that we might choose Major's Hill Park. I am free to admit that I have not made up my mind about the matter yet. This is a very important question. We claim to be a nation, and we are getting big very fast. We are not building for to-day only, but must think of the future. I have, therefore, hesitated to make definite choice of a site. Moreover, I would not like to spend too much money on this museum. At the same time, I feel the responsibility which rests upon this government as it has rested upon previous governments, in that we have a valuable national collection which is exposed to destruction any day. I would not like, however, to spend over half a million for this building. I have no doubt that when I come before the House next year a definite step will have been taken. So far, at least, no money has been spent.

I notice that the minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) seems to be very

much worried over the expenditure of ; money. X have observed the same thing : ever since I have come into the House. I hope his anxiety concerning this expenditure ' or any other is not affecting his health ser- * iously. As to myself and the accommoda- I tion which has been afforded me, I am glad to say that, so far as the room can be made i suitable, I certainly am indebted to the hon. minister for doing everything in his power to provide for me.

Public Works-chargeable to capital-Harbours and rivers, River St. Lawrence Ship Channel, $500,000.
What is the hon. minister going to do with this money ?

This is for the work that is in progress between Quebec and Montreal. We have six elevator dredges, and one large suction dredge lately built at the Poison Iron Works in Toronto. These six dredges work night and day at a cost of $30,000 each. We expect that the large suction dredge to which I have alluded will cost for operation $70,000 a year-and by a year, I mean 185 days. That dredge was tested last fall. Should it, in actual work, respond to our expectations- which are very high, I wish to say-she will work at a very cheap rate. She has a capacity of 2,000 yards an hour; in other words, if she works well, she will dredge nearly nine millions of cubic yards in 185 days.
I do not rely on such large results; but, even if you take off 20 per cent you will see that the dredge will carry on our work very fast and at a very cheap rate. In fact, if it worked to its full capacity the cost of dredging will be only eight-tenths of a cent per yard, that is, if it worked twenty-four hours a day at its full capacity. But I do not expect that result. But even if it only does half that, you will have the dredging done at a cent and a half a yard. We expect that that dredge will do work for one cent a yard. Other modern dredges we have built during the last three or four years are doing work for 3, and 4 cents, while the old dredges did work at a cost of 25 to 30 cents a yard. Now, of this $500,000, $250,000 will be employed for dredges on the St. Lawrence river. The balance of the money will be employed, among other things, to build a new twin screw tug to replace an old one, which will cost in the neighbourhood of $25,000; for the construction of two large dump scows for dredging, $26,000; completion of one scow, $4,000; construction of one flat scow with boiler, $7,000 ; construction of one saw-mill, $15,000 ; construction and equipment of a marine railway, workshops and shipyard, $20,000 ; refitting shipyard, $5,000 ; rebuilding wharf, $3,000. We have $30,000 left for unforeseen expenses.
I will add for the information of the House that we have now in Sorel a shipyard in first-class condition. We are building not only for the St. Lawrence channel, but for the whole country. For instance, we are building at this moment a large dredge for the maritime provinces. We are building it with Canadian labour, we are building it on Canadian soil, we are training Canadian skilled men, we are doing the work as cheaply as it can be done on this side of the ocean. I hope and trust that in the future the government will never be obliged to go elsewhere for our ships or anything else that we can build here. I have endeavoured, as far as my department is concerned, to carry out a policy of building on Canadian soil, either at Sorel or elsewhere, all the plant that was necessary to do our work.
The capacity of the dredge that we are building in the maritime provinces will be 1,800 yards an hour. I may say that I hope it will be the best dredge in the world. It is a very complicated piece of machinery indeed. That is saying a good dleal, but I think I am within the truth in stating that the dredge that we have huilt in Toronto is the most modern dredge that has been built. The dredge for the maritime provinces will be a suction dredge and an elevator dredge at the same time; in other words, when the dredge is called upon to work in soft material we will use the suction machinery, and when it works in harder material we will use the elevator machinery. Now this suction dredge has discharging pipes, and at the same time it will be a hopper dredge. In other words, it will carry away its own material when the weather is stormy, or when the dredge works in some exposed place. I think that dredge will cost in the neighbourhood of $300,000. The Toronto dredge costs $250,000 with the whole equipment. The capacity of the Toronto dredge is 2,000 yards an hour. My opinion is that that dredge will do work for less than a cent a yard.

I am delighted to hear from the Minister of Public Works that we are going to have in Nova Scotia the benefit of the best dredge in the world. I think that will be very satisfactory to the people of Nova Scotia. Being a suction dredge, I hope it will be successful in sucking up some of the shoals we have in the harbours already built. There is a harbour in my own county that cost $80,000 or $82,000, on which no work or any improvement has been made for the last twenty-eight or twenty-nine years. It now needs to be dredged, and I hope before the season is over to see this great dredge doing service in several places in Nova Scotia.

I listened with a good deal of pleasure to the remarks of the hon. the Minister of Public Works, and was glad to learn that he had adopted the plan of building dredges which I recom-

mended to liim three or four years ago. I made a statement in the House some time ago that material in the city of Liverpool for deepening the Mersey had been excavated and removed a certain distance for a sum so small as to seem incredible, T think it was in the neighbourhood of 3 or 8$ cents per cubic yard. I stated also there were improvements likely to be made in the port of New York, and that dredges of the kind they used in Liverpool were going to be adopted in New York. My remarks fell upon appreciative ears, and I find that the Minister of Public Works lias built [DOT]dredges after the Liverpool plan and the New York plan. The hon. gentleman says that material can be moved for eight-tenths of a cent per cubic yard on the St. Lawrence. Possibly that may be so, under the system he tells us he has adopted, of using a hopper dredge having pipes carrying away the material to a certain distance and depositing it on either shore. If he succeeds, he will reduce the cost which has been in the past as high as 28 or 29 cents per cubic yard. Even if he reduces it to 4 or 5 cents, he will accomplish a great deal, and the dredge will well repay the expenditure of money used in building it. These dredges are necessary. The minister has not stated the number of cubic yards that require to be removed on the St. Lawrence and the probable cost of doing that work, or when it is likely to be completed. It is only a year or two since all the requisite improvements upon the St. Lawrence river between Montreal and Quebec have been [DOT]completed. I remember when I was a minister of the Crown that we determined upon selling off those useless dredges which were encamped down at Sorel or in the neighbourhood. There were fifteen or twenty, for which there was no use at all after the improvements on the St. Lawrence river in the way of deepening had been nearly completed. The minister it appears has decided upon having a further depth at the port of Montreal, and I think he is correct. He is extending the depth from twenty-six or twenty-eight feet to thirty feet. I think that is the least we can do if we are going to make Montreal a terminal port for the purpose of transportation, so that a vessel of thirty feet draught will be able to come up to Montreal. As it is nearly six o'clock, I would like the minister to state the amount of material which is required to be excavated for the purpose of accomplishing his object, and the time it will require to do it. It is to be hoped that we may have soon an end of this enormous expenditure we have made in the past for improving navigation between Quebec and Montreal.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
As I will not be here after eight o'clock and as this item may be passed In the meantime, I would like to ask the hon. minister a question or two. He may answer it after eight o'clock, and if I am Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
not here, I will read his answer in the 1 Hansard ' on Monday. I have no objection to a very large amount being voted for the purpose of improving the ship channel between Montreal and Quebec. I will go as far as the hon. minister, or any person in this House in that direction, but when that money is voted I want to know that it is applied to the purpose for which it is voted. I notice by looking at the Auditor General's Report, V-43, a long list of items charged against the money which is voted for this purpose and which have nothing whatever to do with the deepening of a ship channel. I do not suppose these goods are bought by tender because of the very large amounts which, I find, have been paid for them. At Y-43 of the Auditor General's Report I find that Robillard & Co., of Montreal, received $1,271.45 out of the money voted for the improvement of the ship channel, as follows :
Wilton carpet, made and laid, 179-42 yards at $2.75, $493.41.
Two dollars and seventy-five cents for Wilton carpet ! I had my hon. friend (Mr. Birkett) telephone down to one of the large carpet houses in Ottawa and find out the price of the best Wilton carpet. He found out that Wilton carpet is worth from $1.50 to $2.35 a yard. For this same carpet the hon. gentleman has paid $2.75 a yard.
Wilton stair carpet, J, 7 yards at $2.75, 1, 6J yards at $3.25 ; paper, 100 yards at 10c., Brussels carpet, 20 yards at $1, $69.83.
Linoleum, 38 yards at $1.50, 202 yards at 65c., 100 yards at 60c., J24S.30.
Livonea, 614 yards at $1.50 ; table oil cloth, 18i yards, $7.80, $104.55.
Edging, 180 yards at 50c.; bazier, 24 yards at $1.85 ; velvet rugs, 5 at $4, $154.40.
Silk lining, 60J yards at $1.25 ; special loops, 32 at $2; 1 sweeper, $4, $143.31.
This is one of those carpet sweepers that you can buy at apy carpet store for $2.25.
Table cloths, 1 at $20, 1 at $5; tassel hooks, 32 pairs at 35c.; 2 mats, $7.50 ; sundry, $13,95, $57.65.
Making altogether a grand total of $1,271.45, taken out of the money that we voted last year for the improvement and deepening of this ship channel, and for what purpose ? Fitting up, I presume, some tug boat down there, because the hon. gentleman has nothing but dredges and tugs. It may have been for the fitting up of the steamer ' Eureka ' or some other tug. Is that a proper way to spend the money that we have voted for a specific purpose, for the ship channel between Montreal and Quebec ? I turn over to the next page V- 44, and I find that Messrs J. & R. Weir, Montreal, were paid $4,125 for a marine, D., title boiler for tug boat tested to 200 lbs.
After a tender this time.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then the tenders must have been very limited, because I am asking for tenders for a boiler of practically the same capacity and I have a tender which I will bring on Monday for a boiler of 150 h.p. placed in our factory for $1,000.
It is second hand.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: No, it is not second hand ; it is made by the best makers. It is practically a marine boiler and just as good a boiler as there is in any tug boat, and it is made by Messrs Goldie & McCulloch. My hon. friend talks about the price of a tug boat, but if he pays $4,000 for a boiler he will have nothing left for the rest of the equipment. I find in the report of the Auditor General large sums of money, which we have voted, expended in the purchase of goods, bought without tenders and for which two or three prices have been paid to the political friends of the hon. gentleman.

The Prince and Princess of Wales were to visit this country. I thought it was only fair to have a boat equipped on which they might be entertained on the lakes. We were building a boat at Sorel, and I plead guilty to the charge of having equipped her in a way in which I would not have thought of equipping a boat under ordinary circumstances. I quite admit that my officers have spent perhaps $2,000 or $3,000 and perhaps more, but they have done it in providing a boat in a fitting way for an event that was expected to take place.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: For the Minister of Public Works.

The Minister of Public Works has been only twice on board of that boat. I am not a man who travels for pleasure. I have not done it so far. I hope I will be able in my older days to do so, but so far I have not found time to do it. I would like to have that pleasure. This boat was equipped with a certain degree of luxury. Those of my hon. friends who have been ministers of the Crown will freely admit that it is not a bad thing when strangers of distinction come here that we may be enabled to place at their disposal, cars and boats that will not be a disgrace to us. However, I state the case as it is. I quite grant that we have spent a little too much money for ordinary purposes, but there was no boat on the lakes suitable for the expected occasion.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How about the prices that I have quoted ?

I have not bought carpets myself. If my officers have paid too much, I would be very sorry, but my hon. friend has proved on several occasions that he falls into exaggeration. There are carpets and carpets,
as there are men and men. There are some carpets that cost more than other carpets do. I am very glad that my hon. friend has asked the question, because if it had not been explained it would not have looked very well for an ordinary tug boat to be equipped in such a way as that.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if the Prince and Princess of Wales were entertained upon that boat ?

No, because the Prince made up his mind not to travel on the lakes. The programme which was placed in our hands at the time-provided for a trip on the lakes. We had no boat ready, and I think it was not a crime for me to do what I have done.
Is this the 'boat into which the neVv boiler was put ?

No, the new boiler that my hon. friend speaks of is in the right place. My hon. friend speaks of political friends. Will he allow me to state that Mr. Weir, of Montreal, is not a political friend of mine. The order has been given to Mr. Weir after tender in competition with several firms and it was given to a man, who, as I have said, is not a political friend of'mine.
