I was asked by the ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Haggart) to state the amount of dredging required to be done between Quebec and Montreal to give a channel 30 feet deep. I have much pleasure in being able to give the information. There are
24.000.	000 cubic yards to be dredged to accomplish that work. This is made up of
2.000.	000 cubic yards for the Longue Pointe section which is between Longue Pointe and Cap St. Michel. It is estimated that three dredges will do that work in 200 days. The second section is the Contrecceur section and the quantity to be dredged is estimated at 3,000,000 cubic yards. Three

-dredges will do that work in 200 days. There is Lake St. Peter, 18 miles long, and there will be about 19,000,000 cubic yards to be dredged, if we dredge 500 feet wide ; but if we dredge it 450 feet wide there will be between 10,000,000 or 17,000,000 cubic yards of dredging. In the balance of the work between Lake St. Peter and Batiscan, there are 2,800,000 cubic yards. I have no doubt whatever that that work will be completed within the next two years. We have now the equipment to do the work. The ex-minister (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has very truly said that a few years ago we had only very old dredges. In point of fact when the care of the St. Lawrence between Quebec and Montreal was handed over to the government by the Montreal Harbour Commission fti 1888, we had five dredges which were between fourteen and fifteen years old. They had wooden hulls and were altogether out of shape and out of date. You can imagine the condition in which these dredges were when I took office. There was at the time practically only one dredge which was fit for work. That was the dredge ' Laval ' that was built by my predecessor, the Hon. Mr. Ouimet. Since then, thanks to the generosity of parliament, thanks to the attention that has been given by both sides of the House to the transportation question, I have been able to get enough money to build a magnificent fleet of dredges, of stone elevators and tugs. With the dredges we have on hand now we will complete that great national work of dredging the St. Lawrence river 30 feet deep and 450 feet wide between Quebec and Montreal during the next two years, or about that time. As I have said, in Lake St. Peter there are between 10,000,000 and 17,000,000 cubic yards -of dredging if we dredge the channel 450 feet wide. With the big suction dredge that was tested last fall in Toronto I am confident that work will be completed in two years or about that. There were 50 miles to dredge between Quebec and Montreal to make the channel 30 feet deep, but during the last two years we have dredged 19 miles. Therefore, to-day we have 19 miles, 30 feet deep and 450 feet wide, and still wider in the curves. There remains 18 miles in round numbers to be dredged in Lake St. Peter. That work will be done by the big dredge constructed for that special purpose.
How deep is the water in that part ?

It was supposed that we have 274 feet, but I am sorry to say that in reality we have not that depth of water. We are to-day dredging to 30 feet deep, which is to say 4 feet deeper than the lowest water in 1897.
Does this channel fill in ?
'The channel does not fill in.
The ice does not move the boulders into the channel.

No. I have a statement here from Mr. Cosky, the engineer in charge of the work on the St. Lawrence, to the effect that during the last ten or twelve years we have not spent $20,000 to dredge any parts of the channel where there may have been some filling. In point of fact there is no filling. In two years or about that, we will have between Quebec and Montreal a channel 30 feet deep, 450 feet wide in the straight parts and from 500 to 800 feet wide in the curves. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has asked me how much it will cost to complete that work. It is an easy calculation to make. I am asking $500,000 this year. Out of that amount $250,000 will be for the working of the fleet of dredges. We do not expect to spend more next year for that purpose. This year, as last year, I expect that I will ask parliament for large sums of money to build dredges. It is practically our last year of building. Our fleet will then be completed as far as I can see. We will have some little work to do, but the main work of dredge building will be completed. Our expenditure will be then confined to the working of our fleet. There is some work to be done below Quebec. At low tide there will be, I suppose, about one mile to dredge where there is now only 22 or 23 feet of water at low tide. Of course we have betwen 16 feet and 18 feet of tide there. In the calculation I have submitted to the House I did not take into account the Cap la Roche and Richelieu channels, because there we are helped by the tide. I do not say that it will not be found necessary later on to increase the width and depth of that channel, although there is a difficult problem to solve there.
Below Quebec ?

If my hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) will kindly have a look at the map he will find that Cap la Roche is situated above Quebec. WTe have a tide there. When the trade develops later on, the country will see whether it will be necessary or not to do any work there. For the time being we do not find that it is necessary.
What is the nature of the dredging to be done there?
In Lake St. Peter it is sand and clay.
Where do you deposit it ?

In Lake St. Peter we have a big suction dredge with a discharging pipe. The material is dredged out and at the same time deposits it 1,000 feet or even 2,000 feet away from the dredge. We will not have

any trouble there. Elsewhere we are obliged to use scows and tugs to deposit the material wherever it is most convenient to do so.
Did I understand the minister to say that the dredging done tyy this new suction dredge will cost only about one cent a cubic yard ?
Yes, we expect it will not cost more than that.
What is the estimated cost of all the work ?

This year we will spend a quarter of a million; next year there is no reason why we should spend more; the year after we will spend about the same. In round numbers, I do not think, by what I can see, that it will cost more than a quarter of a million dollars each year for working the dredges we have in hand now. In two years I hope we will have about completed the work, but let us say that it takes at the outside three years to do it. I do not expect all the work to be done below Quebec in that time, although there is not much expenditure there.
I did not quite catch what the hon. minister said about the cost of the dredging.
We expect to spend about a quarter of a million dollars each year for three years.

I understood the hon. minister to say that the channel would be thirty feet deep, and I understand that St Peter's channel originally averaged nine feet deep. Does the hon. minister say that the walls of this channel through lake St. Peter, which is to be thirty feet deep, although of clay and sand, will stand as though they were masonry and that no filling in will take place.

When I said it was clay and sand, I should have added that in the channel itself it is only clay. The channel has been dredged for many years and there has been practically no falling in except in one part. We have the experience of the past to go by, and that experience shows us that the walls keep very well because they are of clay. There is sand on the bank, but the channel itself is of clay, and according to our experience that will stand.

There are only about
24,000,000 yards to be dredged between Montreal and Quebec and if the hon. gentleman can do that at less than a cent a yard, that would be $240,000.

I said I expected that the dredging in Lake St. Peter would not cost more than a cent a yard, but I did not say that the dredging in the other parts of the channel could be done for that price, because the material is harder. If my hon. friend wants to know what the dredging costs to-day, he will find it in my report at page 186. During last year the dredging done by the dredge ' Lady Aberdeen ' cost three and a quarter cents per yard in some parts and in others two and half. The dredging done by the ' Lady Minto ' cost in some parts two cents and in others twenty-two cents and in others four and a half and four and three quarters. The * Lady Laurier ' did the work at three and a half cents. The dredging by the dredge * Laval ' cost six cents in some parts. The cost varies according to the material to be dredged. The new dredges are doing the work at three cents and three cents and a half on an average. We have an old dredge, number 11-an old remnant of the past-which cannot do the work at the same prices at all.
What is the name of the new suction dredge built at Toronto ?
I have had the weakness to call it after myself, and I know it will do just as good work.

I understood the hon. gentleman to say that these dredges were specially built for this work and that this work would be completed in three years. What use will there be then for these dredges V Can they be used in other places? Can they be taken through the canals and used In Lake Ontario, dredging out the harbours there ?

There will be no difficulty at all in taking all these dredges to the lakes. Their heaviest draught is between nine and ten feet when light. As to the use that will be made of them, I have not much anxiety. There is any amount of dredging to be done, and there will be no difficulty finding use for them. Of course it will be always necessary to keep some dredges on hand, but if the country should decide to dispose of those dredges, there will be no trouble doing so because they are very fine dredges indeed. Of course I do not know what the future of this country will be. It depends on the men at the helm, it depends on public opinion, but my hon. friends will agree with me that the transportation question is taking hold of public opinion more and more * every day, and I am glad to see so many demands made on me for maps. It proves that public opinion is on the right track at last. On the lakes, I do not hesitate in saying, we are not in it. We are only beginning. All our harbours have to be dredged and equipped, and we are doing that work now. There is that French river scheme of mine, which my hon. friends opposite are afraid of. All I ask

of them is the careful attention which public men are bound to give any new question. That is not ashing too much. And since I am on this subject I may be allowed to ask my hon. friends on both sides how they intend to dispose of the crops of this country in the future. This year we have a crop of 100,000,000 bushels of grain in Manitoba. Now to carry 25,000,000 bushels of grain through the Canadian system of canals would in the fail require a fleet of over fifty Canadian boats, because an American boat cannot navigate between Canadian points, and each boat cannot carry more than 80,000 bushels through our system of canals. Well, we have not the boats, we have not the equipment ready, and it will take some time before we have that equipment. And when we have disposed of those 25,000,000 bushels of Canadian wheat, we have not touched at all the American crop. Duluth, Chicago, Milwaukee-all the great American centres are tributaries to the St. Lawrence. There is only one St. Lawrence river, and thank Cod it flows through Canadian channels. Taking those figures, I ask you not to be frightened when I speak of the French river channel, because you cannot dispose through Canadian channels of your Canadian crop and you cannot touch at all the American crop. We have spent, and we are spending, large amounts to complete the equipment of our harbours. I want to know why we should not spend a good deal more to complete our channels. Is it not better that Canadian and American crops should be carried through the Welland Canal and French river than be carried through American channels. You have to choose between the two. There is no alternative. Some of my Ontario friends say there are some other routes. I do not hesitate in saying once more that if I had a free hand, if I were an absolute ruler such as the Czar of Russia, I would spend a large amount of money to build up all the avenues of trade that lead to the St. Lawrence. I would not hesitate to recommend a careful study of that air line which my hon. friends from Toronto speak of. The Canadian people do not realize the immense possibilities before them.

I do not wish to discuss the subject which the hon. minister has raised, but simply to ask him a question. He has told us the amount of Canadian grain we have to transport to the seaboard. What is the capacity per annum in bushels of the St. Lawrence Canal system, the Grand Trunk Railway, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canada Atlantic at present, and what capacity may they be expected to develop in the course of the next five years V

That is a question my hon. friend is just as competent as I am to answer. This year Hon. Mr. TARTE.
Mr. Booth's system has carried twenty million bushels of grain-not all by the St. Lawrence route, but to American ports also. The Grand Trunk Railway has carried a pretty large quantity. I know that the Canadian Pacific Raihvay carried twelve millions of bushels of wheat to Port William by the close of navigation. Of this quantity seven millions went out by Canadian ports, and five millions by American ports. If the Grand Trunk Railway would make up their mind to double their track between Midland and Montreal, if they* would make up then-mind to give up Portland and carry by the St. Lawrence route-and I hope they will- great things might be expected. As to the Canadian Pacific Railway, they have not in the past carried a great deal of grain by rail. I am glad to say that this year they are doing better than in the past. They have taken grain direct to the winter port. They are not doing it to very great advantage, perhaps, but they are doing it. When the improvement of the French river is carried out, when you have made it possible for the great lake carriers to take grain to Lake Nipissing, which is 360 miles from Montreal, you will necessarily see a vast accumulation of trade-not only grain, but other trade-at that point. From Lake Nipissing, the Canadian Pacific Railway, during the winter months, will convey the freight to our winter ports. When I speak of the St. Lawrence route, I do not speak only of Montreal, Three Rivers and Quebec, but of the St. Lawrence as a whole-of our winter ports just as much as any others. I believe the Canadian people are realizing more and more that, if we are to be a nation, we must make ourselves independent of our neighbours, not only industrially and commercially, but also in respect of transportation. I have never felt so strongly as I do now that Canadian people should be their own masters. Our American neighbours are, perhaps, friendly to us, but I think we had better be our own friends and consider the ways and means by which we may remain masters of our own destiny. And it is because I have given some attention to this transportation question that I ask hon. members on both sides of this House to study it-I will not say as much as I have done, because I do not boast of having studied more than others-but to give this question the attention that, in my opinion, it deserves.

This question is the most important one before the country.	I may differ in opinion from
many members of this House, but my opinion is that, while, perhaps, these expenditures are necessary they will not be operative in the end. I believe, that, situated as we are, with the climate that we have, ultimately we must come to it that the exportation of the great volume of products of this country must be carried on from ports that during summer and winter are alike. It might

be worthy of consideration by this parliament whether the sums of money that are being voted could not be set aside to help tiie railways to make the freight rates as small as possible, so that all the year around the freight could go to the lower provinces to be exported. Of course, for a certain length of time in the year after the crop is gathered, there can be a good deal of exportation by waterway. But that is only for a short time at best, and we cannot look forward to any change in that respect. Might it not be worth our while to look at the larger question ? Is it of sufficient importance that all this grain raised in Canada shall be exported from a Canadian port ?
Hear, hear-.

Then, if it is, we must see to it that we have methods of transportation in Canada and exportation from Canada that can be used all the year round. I have faith in Canada. I believe that not only shall we increase as we have been increasing, but that every increase now will help to make greater our ratio of increase for the future. The more people we get, the more grain we raise, the more we do, the more we produce, the more rapid will be our increase in the future. I believe in the St. Lawrence route. I believe it is necessary, even if they should fail in their immediate purposes, to make these expenditures. A nation often has to spend money to demonstrate a truth, it has often to spend money to find out what is the real value of an idea strongly held by many of its people. But I am firmly convinced that we must come to it that the lower provinces, with their ports open all the year round, must be the points at which we export as well as import. Nova Scotia is the vestibule of this Dominion. Geography is in our favour; and I believe that as we grow-and we shall grow-it will be seen that it is in this way that all our products must go and come. As I say, it may be necessary now to expend our money in the way proposed. In any case, it will do no harm to have an alternate way of carrying, subsidiary to the great system by which freight can be carried and exported all the year round. It is like the money spent on our canals, which was thought to make them all that was required, but which had to be supplemented with more money to deepen them-and I believe that, if those canals are to be really effective. we must deepen them again. We are only making these tentative steps in our history. I believe, however, that the country will yet come to the conclusion that the really useful expenditure is that which will make it possible for the producer in Canada to ship his products over a Canadian route and by a Canadian port, and that rather than spend our money continuously in other ways, we should devote our resources 19
to the carrying out of this idea. So strong am I in this position, that, while I am in full sympathy with the expenditures made, if they are necessary, I believe, looking at it in the broader light of geography and climate, we must ship from ports where neither frost nor tide will interfere with work whatever the season may be.

I have before me a map which bears the name of the hon. Minister of Public Works. I am trying to get at the hon. minister's point of view. May I inquire whether he has ever considered the idea of having a harbour on the north shore of Georgian Bay near the mouth of the French river, for the purpose of allowing the Canadian Pacific Railway to tap it at that point and transfer grain ? Then, I would like to ask how much sooner in the autumn the French river is closed in the winter by ice than is the Welland Canal ?

I am very glad to be in a position to give a definite answer to my hon. friend (Mr. Kemp). I was asked a few days ago what the distance was between the Soo line and a port on Georgian Bay, and I was not able to give the exact distance at the moment. The distance between the Soo line and the nearest point on Georgian Bay is 90 miles. There are great engineering difficulties-
What is the greatest distance ?

The distance from the Soo line to the Georgian Bay is ninety miles. That is the distance that would have to be covered if a branch line were built. Now my hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) has a map in his hand. I hope my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Fraser), has one also. Let them look at the different centres of trade. Let them look at Fort William, which is a point from which our Canadian grain is carried. Now let them look at Duluth, Milwaukee, Chicago. From Fort William to North Bay the distance is 473 miles; from North Bay to Montreal, 317 miles, I speak of nautical miles. That makes altogether 890 miles. From Fort William to New York there are 1,182 miles, making 292 miles of difference in favour of the Canadian route. Now from New York to Liverpool there are 3,105 miles; from Montreal to Liverpool there are 2,773 miles, a difference of 332 miles. This is for the French river route. From Fort William to Port Colborne there are 737 miles; from Port Colborne to Montreal there are 321 miles, in all 1,058 miles. From Fort William to Buffalo there are 750 miles; from Buffalo to New York by the Erie Canal. 500 miles, or 1,250 miles in all, making 200 miles difference in favour of the Canadian route. But if my hon. friends will look at the figures published on the map they will find that, taking Fort William, Duluth, Milwau-



kee and Chicago as shipping points to Montreal or New York, there is a difference in round numbers of 300 miles in favour of our Canadian route. Now adding the difference there is between Montreal and Liverpool and that between New York and Liverpool, you will find in round numbers a difference of 600 miles in favour of our Canadian route. Now I want to know why we should not divert a vast quantity of trade from all these centres through the Canadian route.
But you are now pointing out the disadvantages of the Canadian route.
Not at all. How so 7
You are speaking of all water Canadian routes. There are half a dozen routes partly rail and partly water that are 600 miles shorter than the all Canadian route.

I do not admit that. When I speak of the French river route, I speak of an all water route, not of a railway route, because Buffalo is our objective opponent, if I may so speak. Let us take Buffalo, and let us see what is the difference between Buffalo and North Bay, for instance. Between Montreal and North Bay-I do not now speak of nautical miles-there are 364 railway miles; between Buffalo and New York there are 445 railway miles. Between North Bay and Montreal, the Canadian Pacific Railway is running on the down grade, and can haul just as many cars as the New York Central does, and the Canadian Pacific Railway would have nearly 100 miles less. I want to know why we cannot acquire a vast quantity of trade at North Bay on Lake Nipissing and carry it In the winter months to the port of St. John 7

Would not that argument apply to other points on the Georgian Bay 7 Why could not other railways accumulate freight in. the fall at other ports on the Georgian Bay 7 I am only making these suggestions to the minister to ascertain how deeply he has looked into the qualifications of these other ports on the Georgian Bay. He has given the figures correctly. The distance from North Bay to Montreal is 364 miles. What is the distance between Parry Harbour, a port that not a dollar need be spent on now- what is the distance between Parry Harbour and Montreal by rail 7 What is the distance between Midland and Montreal by rail 7 These are two splendid harbours already provided on Georgian Bay. What is the distance from Collingwood to Montreal by rail 7 What is the distance from Owen Sound to Montreal by rail 7 We want the minister to give us all the infor-

mation so that we may study it out carefully; and when he comes down this session or the next session, and asks parliament for an appropriation which will eventually aggregate $5,000,000 to make this French river navigable from Georgian Bay to the North Bay, we, having all the facts before us, may bp able to discuss it intelligently with him. When he completes the work of making the French river and Lake Nipissing navigable to North Bay he will find that North Bay is five miles further away from the Sault than Parry Harbour, and ten miles further away than Midland. These two harbours already provided on Georgian Bay are nearer to the Soo, the common point from which all the vessels must start after they come through Lake Superior. Both these ports are nearer to the Soo than North Bay will be after this enormous expenditure has been made upon it.
Now, I am not saying that this expenditure ought not to be made, but surely we all, on both sides of the House, have a right to the fullest possible information as to these distances. And let me tell the hon. gentleman that this table of sailing distances which is printed on the lower right hand corner of this map may be misleading. I do not of course think it was put in there at all for that purpose. I think, too, that if he is going to ask us to consider this French river route the information contained on this map should be implemented. We should have the distances from Fort William to Collingwood and from Collingwood to Montreal, and from Toronto to Montreal or Quebec by water. We should have some data, some information as to the relative cost of carriage by water as compared with carriage by rail. The hon. gentleman who addressed us a few minutes ago said, what I believe to be substantially correct, that in the future a very large proportion of the grain grown in the west will find its way to the east almost altogether by rail or very largely by rail. We must not overlook the fact that at present we are engaged in a very large expenditure to complete our all water Canadian route. We are engaged in the work of making a harbour at Port Colborne, the Lake Erie entrance to the Welland Canal, and before that work is completed a very large sum will have to be expended. That route is unfortunately handicapped by being 600 miles, on the round trip, longer than these routes that are being spoken of. North Bay, Depot Harbour, Midland and Collingwood, but it has the advantage of being an all water route.
Now, if we want to get the best possible results for the producers of this country we must not tie ourselves up completely to railways. We must give our farmers the advantage, and our shippers the advantage of more than one avenue for conveying the produce of this country to the

seaboard. We have in the North Bay route, when it is completed, a line that obliges a land haul of between 300 and 400 miles to Montreal. We have as against that our present all water route, handicapped, as I have pointed out, by being, for the round trip 600 miles, in round figures, longer than these other routes, but with the advantage of an all water carriage. We can have another route by making a portage railway from Meaford, or from Collingwood, or from some point on the Georgian Bay, to Bake Ontario, which will give us a very much shorter water route, and which will give us just as short a route from Sault Ste. Marie to Montreal as any of these other routes, and with only seventy miles or eighty miles at most of land carriage. I think in fairness to the members of this House all the facts in connection with all these propositions-and the minister says he has considered this proposition of a portage railway from Georgian Bay down to Toronto- 1 think all the facts should be laid before us so that we may be able to bring the best possible intelligence to bear before we are asked to come to a conclusion. I want to assure the hon. gentleman that there is nothing sectional, nothing narrow, in the opposition, if he can call it opposition, that we are offering to this French river proposition. We are not necessarily opposing that scheme because it means an expenditure of $5,000,000 away up in the north. But we want to be perfectly satisfied before we vote for that expenditure that it is the best possible way of expending the money, and will produce the best possible results in the years that are to come for those people who are going out west in such large numbers to make themselves homes. The hon. minister must not overlook this fact, that, as he has pointed out, there is a down grade from North Bay to Montreal, so that consequently, there must be an up grade going back. If he desires to see the Canadian inland marine prospering, if he desires to see large additions made to the tonnage of that marine he must give vessels all possible facilities to go up to the head of Lake Ontario and it is only policy carefully to consider at what point on Lake Ontario these vessels will be likely to get the largest and greatest number of return cargoes. My idea is that the making of a national port at Montreal will not completely solve this transportation problem.
Hear, hear.
Of course it is only my own opinion, but I believe that the old port of Quebec will eventually become the national port of this Dominion.

Hear, hear; one of them.
